Chicago has a large [Irish American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_American "Irish American") population, with many still residing on the South Side. The early years of Chicago coincided with the significant rise in Irish immigration in the 1830s and 1840s. Some Irish already lived in Chicago when it was incorporated as a city in 1837. In the next few years Irish numbers grew rapidly, particularly after the arrival of refugees from the [Great Famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_(Ireland) "Great Famine (Ireland)"). By 1850 Irish immigrants accounted for about one-fifth of the city's population. Many of the city's politicians are descendants of this group, including previous mayor Richard M. Daley. The Irish were able to assert themselves in politics due to their large population but also the fact that they knew English and that – thanks to the geographic position of Ireland on the periphery of Europe – they did not have ancestral ethnic rivalries. As the old saying went, _"A Lithuanian won't vote for a Pole, and a Pole won't vote for a Lithuanian. A German won't vote for either of them. But all three will vote for a turkey. – an Irishman." Only the WASPs hated the Irish, and the WASPs all lived on the North Shore."_[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-29) The Irish gained entry to Chicago's Fire and Police Departments and have kept family traditions of participation in these units. The Irish laid the foundations for many of the city's Roman Catholic churches, schools and hospitals. The Irish are still very active in the city's politics.

[Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Americans "German Americans") have constituted a major portion of ethnic whites in Chicago since the beginning of the city's history. When the Great Plains opened up for settlement in the 1830s and 1840s, many German immigrants stopped in Chicago to earn additional money before moving West to claim a homestead. Those with skills in demand could—and often did—stay. From 1850, when Germans constituted one-sixth of Chicago's population, until the turn of the 20th century, people of German descent constituted the largest ethnic group in the city, followed by Irish, Poles, and Swedes. In 1900, 470,000 Chicagoans—one out of every four residents—had either been born in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") or had a parent born there. Although their numbers dropped because of reduced [emigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emigration "Emigration") from [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") and because [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") had made it unpopular to acknowledge one's German heritage, 22 percent of Chicago's population still did so in 1920.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-30) One of the most distinct of these German groups were the [Volga Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volga_Germans "Volga Germans"), or [ethnic Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_Germans "Ethnic Germans") having lived along the [Volga River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volga_River "Volga River") in [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"). They largely clustered in [Jefferson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Park,_Chicago "Jefferson Park, Chicago") on the city's [Northwest Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Side,_Chicago "Northwest Side, Chicago"), coming to the area mostly between the years 1907–1920. By 1930 450 families of [Volga German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volga_German "Volga German") heritage were living in the Jefferson Park area, most of whom originated from _Wiesenseite_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-31) Chicago also hosts the headquarters of the largest [Lutheran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism "Lutheranism") body in the United States, the [Evangelical Lutheran Church in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Lutheran_Church_in_America "Evangelical Lutheran Church in America").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-Contact_Us-32)[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The city has one of the largest [Assyrian diaspora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrian_Diaspora "Assyrian Diaspora") populations, with the [Assyrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrian_people "Assyrian people") community of Metropolitan Chicago numbering as many as 80,000.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-33) The [Patriarchal see](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriarchal_see "Patriarchal see") of the [Assyrian Church of the East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrian_Church_of_the_East "Assyrian Church of the East") was based in Chicago for several decades up until 2015 when it was moved to [Erbil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erbil "Erbil"). There is also a smaller [Armenian diaspora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_diaspora "Armenian diaspora") in the Greater Chicago area, numbering around 10,000. There are seven [Armenian Apostolic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Apostolic_Church "Armenian Apostolic Church") Churches in Chicagoland.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-35)

The city is the home to a large [Romanian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_American "Romanian American") community with more than 100,000.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-archive.org-36)

Polish people have been prevalent from the city's early history, but the largest waves of immigration were in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; they have been influential in the economic and social development of Chicago. This is one of the most important centers of [Polonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_diaspora "Polish diaspora"). The [Taste of Polonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_of_Polonia "Taste of Polonia") Festival in [Jefferson Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Park,_Chicago "Jefferson Park, Chicago") celebrates Polish culture annually on Labor Day weekend.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-usaweekend.com-37) The [Southwest Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Side_(Chicago)#Southwest_Side "South Side (Chicago)") is home to the largest concentration of [Gorals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorals "Gorals") ([Carpathian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpathian_Mountains "Carpathian Mountains") highlanders) outside [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"). The southwest side is also the location of the [Polish Highlanders Alliance of North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Highlanders_Alliance_of_North_America "Polish Highlanders Alliance of North America"). Many Polish churches are found in Chicago, built in the [Polish Cathedral style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Cathedral_style "Polish Cathedral style") of architecture. Some can be seen from the Kennedy Expressway, other roadways, and public transportation routes, as well as from the neighborhood streets.

Chicago has one of the largest concentrations of [Italian Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_American "Italian American") in the US, with more than 500,000 living in the metropolitan area.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-38) Chicago has the third largest [Italian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_American "Italian American") population in the United States, behind only [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"). Chicago's Italian community has historically been based along the Taylor Street and [Grand Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Avenue_(Chicago) "Grand Avenue (Chicago)") corridors on the West Side of the city. There are also significant Italian populations scattered throughout the city and surrounding suburbs.

Other prevalent [European ethnic groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_ethnic_groups "European ethnic groups") include the [Czechs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_American "Czech American"), and [Ukrainians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_American "Ukrainian American"). At the turn of the 20th century, Chicago was the third-largest [Czech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_American "Czech American") city in the world, after [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague "Prague") and [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-39) There are approximately 14,000 Ukrainians living within the Chicago city limits.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-40) Chicago has a small community of [Swedish Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_American "Swedish American"), who make up 0.9% of Chicago's population and number at 23,990.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-41) After the [Great Chicago Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1871_Great_Chicago_Fire "1871 Great Chicago Fire"), many Swedish carpenters helped to rebuild the city, which led to the saying "the Swedes built Chicago."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-42) Swedish influence is evident in [Andersonville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgewater,_Chicago#Andersonville "Edgewater, Chicago") on the far north side.

The city has a large population of [Bulgarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarians "Bulgarians"), [Lithuanians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanian_people "Lithuanian people"),[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-43)[Croats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatians "Croatians"), [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews_in_Chicago "Jews in Chicago"), [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks "Greeks") and [Serbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbs "Serbs"). Chicago has a sizeable [Romanian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_American "Romanian American") community,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-archive.org-36)As of 2018[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Chicago&action=edit), the Lithuanian population is over 100,000 and was formerly over 300,000; the world's oldest continuously published Lithuanian-language newspaper _[Draugus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draugus?action=edit&redlink=1 "Draugus (page does not exist)")_ is based in Chicago.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-lith-44) The city is the seat of the [Evangelical Covenant Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Covenant_Church "Evangelical Covenant Church") and the [Evangelical Lutheran Church in America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Lutheran_Church_in_America "Evangelical Lutheran Church in America").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-Contact_Us-32)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-45)

Chicago has the third-largest [South Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia "South Asia") population in the United States, especially many [Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_American "Indian American"), Bangladeshi and [Pakistanis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistani_American "Pakistani American"). The [Devon Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devon_Avenue_(Chicago) "Devon Avenue (Chicago)") corridor on the far north side is one of the largest South Asian neighborhoods/markets in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"). As of the [2010 Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_census "2010 United States census"), Chicago has the third-largest [Puerto Rican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Ricans_in_the_United_States "Puerto Ricans in the United States") population in the continental United States,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-46) after [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), and the fourth largest Mexican population in the United States after [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles,_California "Los Angeles, California"), [San Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio,_Texas "San Antonio, Texas"), and [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-About_Us-47) There are about 185,000 Arabs in Cook County with another 75,000 in the five surrounding counties. Chicago is the center of the [Palestinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestinian_people "Palestinian people") and [Jordanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan "Jordan") immigrant communities in the United States,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-49) and additionally has a large [Assyrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrian_people "Assyrian people") population.

There is a substantial [Romani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romani_people "Romani people") community in Chicago. The Roma first came to Chicago during the large waves of Southern and Eastern European immigration to the United States in the 1880s until World War I. They were following Serbian and Hungarian immigrants who found work in the steel mills and factories of the city.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-50)

### Bosnian population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Chicago&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Bosnian population")]

Further information: [Bosnians in Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnians_in_Chicago "Bosnians in Chicago")

The first [Bosnians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnians "Bosnians") settled in Chicago in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, joining other immigrants seeking better opportunities and better lives. As the former Yugoslavia continued to find its identity as a nation over the last century, the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina sought stability and new beginnings in the city of Chicago many intending to return to their homeland. Bosnian Muslims were early leaders in the establishment of Chicago's Muslim community. In 1906, they established Dzemijetul Hajrije (The Benevolent Society) of Illinois to preserve the community's religious and national traditions as well as to provide mutual assistance for funerals and illness. The organization established chapters in [Gary, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary,_Indiana "Gary, Indiana"), in 1913, and [Butte, Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butte,_Montana "Butte, Montana"), in 1916, and is the oldest existing Muslim organization in the United States.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-51) The Bosnians were the first Muslims in the United States to incorporate an Islamic Association in 1906 in Chicago, Illinois.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-52) Today, Chicago and [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis") are tied for the largest Bosnian population in the United States and the largest Bosnian population outside of Europe, with 70,000 in each city.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-54) 40,000 of them came as refugees during the 1990s and early 2000s.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-55)

This marked the second consecutive year of population increase, while still not yet returning to the official Census 2000 population level. There were more than 1,061,928 households, of which 28.9% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 35.1% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage "Marriage") living together, 18.9% had a female householder with no husband present, and 40.4% were non-families. Of all households, 32.6% were made up of individuals, and 8.7% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.67 and the average family size was 3.50.

Of the city population, 26.2% were under the age of 18, 11.2% were from 18 to 24, 33.4% were from 25 to 44, 18.9% from 45 to 64, and 10.3% 65 years of age or older. The median age was 32 years. For every 100 females there were 94.2 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 91.1 males.

The median income for a household in the city was $38,625, and the median income for a family was $42,724. Males had a median income of $35,907 versus $30,536 for females. The [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income "Per capita income") for the city was $20,175. Below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_line "Poverty line") were 19.6% of the population and 16.6% of the families. Of the total population, 28.1% of those under the age of 18 and 15.5% of those 75 and older were living below the poverty line.

Population estimates in 2008 put the number of people in the city proper at 2,853,114, while suburban populations continue to grow, with estimates at 9,785,747 for the combined city and suburbs.

## LGBT population

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Chicago&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: LGBT population")]

Main article: [LGBT culture in Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_culture_in_Chicago "LGBT culture in Chicago")

Chicago has one of the largest [LGBTQ+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ+ "LGBTQ+") populations in the United States. In 2015, roughly 4% of the population identified as LGBTQ+. [[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-59) As of 2020, over 15,000 same-sex couples have wed in [Cook County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_County "Cook County") alone since the legalization of same-sex marriage in the State of Illinois in 2013.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Chicago#cite_note-60)
